transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-27
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood CSM), John Rivera (Orion VP Eng), Sara Gomez (Orion SRE), Amir Khan (Orion Security), Lena Park (Orion Product), Marco Diaz (Orion Ops)

Summary: brief check-in to review postmortem actions from the April 15 outage that impacted Orion Health nightly batch jobs and user-facing inference. Discussed root cause (KV cache eviction + autoscaler race), mitigations (runtime patch, routing fallback fixes), monitoring and synthetic tests, and next steps for canary rollout and compliance docs.

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we wanted to go through the postmortem follow up and make sure the actions are clear, i'll kick it off, Ethan do you want to summarize the tech root cause?
[00:27] Ethan Chen: yeah, sure so to recap, on 4-15 we saw increased tail latency and then sustained OOMs on a subset of dedicated hosts, which caused routing to failover incorrectly, um the quick version is the KV cache eviction logic had a race when under spike and continuous batching, it ended up evicting live entries and then the runtime tried to refill causing repeated mem growth, eventually the process restarted and some requests hit a fallback tier that didn't have the same model variant which increased latency and failed some auth checks.
[00:56] Sara Gomez: and to add, we saw the scaling policy not trigger in time because the autoscaler threshold was based on cpu not memory, so memory growth wasn't surfaced early enough, so by the time we spawned new pods the routes had already been marked degraded.
[01:18] John Rivera: that matches our logs, and the customer impact was the nightly inference batch for claims processing ran incomplete, plus a handful of clinician-facing requests timed out. need that fixed.
[01:32] Ethan Chen: agreed. root cause list in the postmortem was KV eviction race, autoscaler thresholds, and routing fallback misconfiguration. we have a proposed patch that changes the eviction to be copy-on-write and adds a guard to prevent incremental mem leaks, also plan to add a canary and rollback hook.
[01:58] Amir Khan: quick security note, any change to the runtime that touches cache or memory, we need to ensure it doesn't affect our KMS integration or key lifecycle, and audit logs must remain intact, otherwise compliance will raise flags. do we have a change plan?
[02:22] Maya Patel: yes, we will provide the patch as a build, and we will run a canary in your dedicated pool first, also we'll share the updated security review notes and SOC2 artifacts, Ethan will own the build, Priya will manage the runbook updates.
[02:45] Lena Park: what about the routing fallback config? is that part of this patch or a separate change?
[02:56] Ethan Chen: routing change is separate but closely related — it's a config fix to ensure that when a host is unhealthy we route to a compatible model variant and not downgrade to an incompatible model. we'll push that as a config change first, it's lower risk.
[03:20] Marco Diaz: can you say more about the compatibility checks? sometimes the model variants have different tokenization or prompt handling which caused failures.
[03:34] Ethan Chen: yeah good point — the compatibility check now verifies model family, tokenizer version, and max sequence length before fallback. if it doesn't match we fail closed to avoid silent incorrect results, which we know is better for Orion's use case.
[03:58] Sara Gomez: i want synthetic tests that replicate our nightly batch patterns, including long sequences and bursts, so we can validate the canary under realistic load.
[04:18] Ethan Chen: we'll provide a testing harness and a sample workload file; we noted in the postmortem the sequence length distribution is skewed compared to typical web requests, so we'll calibrate.
[04:36] John Rivera: timeline — when can we expect the patch in our environment?
[04:43] Maya Patel: target is 2026-04-30 for a canary build, full rollout pending canary results the following week.
[04:52] John Rivera: okay that's reasonable.

Topics/Discussion:
[05:10] (Discussion on monitoring and alerts)
[05:10] Priya Singh: current alerts are mostly token rate and 5xxs, we didn't have a memory growth alert threshold; i'm proposing adding a high-memory alert and a sustained-increase signal that triggers before autoscaler.
[05:31] Sara Gomez: yes please, add both memory absolute and growth-rate alerts, and integrate with our pager duty escalation. we had 30 minutes of degraded state before paging.
[05:45] Priya Singh: noted, i'll add to runbook.

[06:00] (Clarifications on canary plan)
[06:00] Ethan Chen: canary steps: 1) build with KV eviction guard 2) deploy to a two-host canary in your dedicated pool 3) run synthetic batch and live traffic shadowing for 24 hours 4) check memory metrics and latency 5) if green, expand to 20% traffic then full.
[06:30] Sara Gomez: for the shadowing step, can we mask PII and use replaced tokens? we need to make sure PHI isn't leaked to any logs.
[06:43] Ethan Chen: yes we'll use token redaction and sandbox keys. we will not send raw PHI to external telemetry.

[07:05] (Runbook and escalation)
[07:05] Priya Singh: updated runbook will include immediate mitigation steps: restart host, drain and rebuild with new build, route to fallback region, and contact points — we'll also include the command set to see kv cache stats.
[07:28] Marco Diaz: pls include exact kubectl commands and where to fetch the heapdump, that was missing last time.
[07:40] Priya Singh: yep, will add.

[08:00] (Compliance and security discussion)
[08:00] Amir Khan: two asks: 1) provide SOC2 evidence the change doesn't impact encryption-at-rest and key rotation, 2) confirm audit-log retention for requests and who can access them.
[08:18] Maya Patel: we have SOC2 materials and the change is only in runtime memory handling, not in key paths, but we'll produce test evidence; i'll share the security link and a short checklist.
[08:34] Amir Khan: also, ensure that logs we collect for debugging exclude PII by default and that SREs have limited access.
[08:44] Priya Singh: agreed, RBAC review is part of the runbook update.

[09:05] (Discussion of long-term reliability improvements)
[09:05] Ethan Chen: long-term we recommend adding synthetic canaries for nightly batch windows, an autoscaler tuning project to consider memory-aware scaling, and a KV cache rework for multi-tenant safety. also suggest a model compatibility matrix as part of the deployment pipeline.
[09:36] John Rivera: for us, the most important is no silent fallback to incompatible variants and predictable batch completion. the rest are nice-to-haves.

[10:00] (Objections and tradeoffs)
[10:00] Lena Park: what is the estimated impact on latency and cost if we change to fail-closed on incompatible fallback?
[10:12] Ethan Chen: you may see a small increase in 5xxs instead of silent wrong responses; cost should be negligible but we can quantify. failing closed reduces incorrect outputs but may require application retry logic.
[10:36] Maya Patel: we can run an A/B on this in staging.

[11:00] (Benchmarks and verification)
[11:00] Ethan Chen: we'll run the synthetic workload and provide a spreadsheet with latency and memory over time, plus a CSV of errors. we'll share the link: https://redwood.internal/benchmarks/orion-2026-04 (placeholder).
[11:20] Sara Gomez: please include the raw traces for our ops team.

[12:00] (Recap and commitments)
[12:00] Maya Patel: recap — patch and canary build by 4/30, synthetic tests by Orion by 5/4, runbook updated by 5/3, security docs and SOC2 evidence by 4/29, follow-up review 5/6. action owners reflected in the notes.
[12:34] John Rivera: thanks, please prioritize the canary, and if any blocker pop up escalate to my team immediately.
[12:45] Maya Patel: will do. thanks everyone.
